items.stem: A page takes 200 ms to load for users in Manila and 900 ms for users in Frankfurt. The server is in Manila and its code takes 40 ms in both cases. What explains most of the difference?

options.text: Each round trip takes longer over the greater distance, and loading a page needs several of them.
options.feedback: DNS lookup, connection setup, encryption setup and the request each need at least one round trip, and each is longer for Frankfurt.

options.text: The server runs slower code for Frankfurt users.
options.feedback: The server's code takes the same 40 ms for both groups.

options.text: The server has less memory for users far away.
options.feedback: Memory is not shared out by distance. The difference comes from travel time.

options.text: Browsers in Europe are slower than browsers in Manila.
options.feedback: Nothing about the browser changes with location. The network path does.

items.stem: Before you try it: you double the one-way latency from 5 ms to 10 ms. What happens to the time spent in the server handler and to the network time?

options.text: The handler stays at 40 ms and the network time roughly doubles.
options.feedback: The handler's time does not depend on distance. Each round trip gets longer, so the network part grows almost in proportion.

options.text: Both the handler time and the network time double.
options.feedback: Your code takes the same time wherever the user is.

options.text: The handler time doubles and the network time stays the same.
options.feedback: This reverses the effect. Distance changes network time and has no effect on how long your code runs.
The network time changes because each round trip takes twice as long.

items.try: Move the one-way latency slider from 5 ms to 10 ms and compare the timing chart.

items.stem: A company moves its Manila site to a bigger server. The handler time drops from 40 ms to 10 ms. What happens to the wait of a user in Berlin?

options.text: It improves by about 30 ms, but the round trips still make up most of the wait.
options.feedback: A faster server shortens only the handler step. The setup steps still need several long round trips.
Only the handler step got faster. The network steps are unchanged.

options.text: It does not change at all.
options.feedback: The handler time did drop by 30 ms, so the total drops by that amount.

options.text: It gets worse, because a bigger server is further away.
options.feedback: A bigger server in the same place is no further away. The distance is unchanged.
